sections.h2: Where do I record a deed in Hancock County, Ohio?
sections.html:
Deeds for Hancock County property are recorded at the Recorder's office, 300 S. Main Street, Room 23, Findlay, Ohio 45840. The phone is 419-424-7091. The office is open Monday through Friday, 8:30 am to 4:30 pm, and recording for the day stops at 4:00 pm. A document handed over after that is recorded the next business day.

You can walk in, mail the paperwork or send it electronically. A mailed package should hold the document, the payment, a self-addressed envelope for the return, any conveyance forms if the deed transfers ownership, and written recording instructions if the filing needs them.

sections.h2: What is Hancock County like, and what does that mean for deed activity?
sections.html:
Hancock County is a northwest Ohio county of 531 square miles of land, with Findlay as the seat and largest city. It was organized in 1828 from the southern portion of Wood County, and it is named for John Hancock. It borders Wood, Seneca, Wyandot, Hardin, Allen, Putnam and Henry counties.

The Census Bureau counted 74,920 people in 2020 and estimated 75,034 for July 1, 2025, so the county has been close to flat. Roughly 70.8% of households own the home they live in.

  • Typical home value among owners: $204,700 for 2020 to 2024.
  • Median household income: $73,141, with 9.0% of people in poverty.
  • Housing units: 34,342, and 361 building permits were issued in 2025.
  • Average commute: 18.0 minutes, shorter than in Hamilton County.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts for Hancock County. Wikipedia supplies the county's founding and neighbors.

sections.h2: What does the Hancock County Recorder charge in 2025 and later?
sections.html:
Since January 1, 2025, the first two pages cost $39 and each added page costs $8. The Recorder's fee page ties the $5 increase to Senate Bill 94, which allows a preservation surcharge, and points to ORC 317.32.

ItemFee listed by the Recorder
First two pages (deed, mortgage, lease, other)$39
Each additional page$8
Marginal entry$4
Copies, assisted, per page$2
Copies, unassisted, per page$0.15
Non-conforming document (ORC 317.114)$20
Federal tax lien, and its release$5 and $3

Source: Hancock County Recorder fee schedule page. The office takes cash or check only and does not take credit cards. Write checks to the Hancock County Recorder, and use a separate check for the Auditor's payment.

sections.h2: What does the Hancock County Auditor collect on a deed transfer?
sections.html:
The Recorder's FAQ states that the Auditor's conveyance fee is $3.00 per thousand and the transfer fee is $0.50 per parcel. A deed that changes ownership goes through the Auditor's office before it reaches the Recorder, and the two offices work together so the transfer and the recording match.

Under the statute the buyer, or the buyer's representative, files the value statement with the Auditor. ORC 319.202 defines value as the full consideration paid or to be paid, including any mortgage or vendor's lien on the land, and it makes it unlawful to willfully falsify the value. When the transfer is exempt, only a statement of the reason is required.

Ask the Hancock County Auditor which forms apply if the land carried a homestead reduction or an agricultural valuation, because the statute asks the seller about both.

sections.h2: What happens if a deed is not recorded in Hancock County?
sections.html:
An unrecorded deed loses ground against a later buyer. Under ORC 5301.25, a deed must be recorded in the county where the land lies, and until it is recorded it is fraudulent as to a subsequent purchaser in good faith who had no knowledge of it.

That statute also covers surveys. If a survey was made of land being conveyed, the Auditor requires the surveyor's name to appear in the deed, with a line such as "A survey of this property was made by" followed by the name.

  • Record soon after closing, not months later.
  • Keep the Auditor's endorsement and the Recorder's return copy together.
  • Check that the legal description matches the prior deed.

sections.h2: Why does the Hancock County Recorder index every document?
sections.html:
The Recorder's page says the office must keep land records that are current, legible and easy to reach, and indexing is how a searcher finds each one. Good indexing lets an examiner build a chain of title, the history of ownership, and see any debts or encumbrances against the property.

The users it names include the general public, attorneys, historians, genealogists and land title examiners. Some counties also hold land registered under the Torrens Act, and the Recorder explains that those boundaries are certified and the title is guaranteed by a state insurance fund. For a Hancock County seller, the practical point is that a clean deed history makes a title search quick, and a gap in it slows closing.

sections.h2: How did Hancock County's townships shape its parcels?
sections.html:
Hancock County began in 1828 as Findlay Township alone, and Amanda and Welfare (now Delaware) townships followed that April. Jackson came in 1829, Liberty and Marion in December 1830, and Big Lick, Blanchard and Van Buren in 1831. Washington, Union and Eagle were laid out in 1832, Cass and Portage in 1833, Pleasant in 1835, Orange in 1836, Madison in 1840 and Allen in 1850.

In 1845 the county gave up part of its southeast corner to the new Wyandot County. A rural parcel's legal description often names its township, so deeds for farmland outside Findlay will cite those units. Make sure the description in your new deed matches the one in the deed you received.

sections.h2: How do I search Hancock County land records?
sections.html:
The Recorder's online search holds documents recorded and imaged from January 1, 1985 to the present, and historical indexes can be viewed online as well. Enter names last name first, such as Doe John, and enter companies as they normally appear.

A search cannot be run by parcel number at the Recorder's office. You need the owner's name and the legal description. If you lack either one, start at the Hancock County Auditor's website to find the owner and parcel details, then return to the Recorder.

The county is indexed alphabetically online only for 1985 to the present, and anything earlier has to be searched in the office. The Recorder will also provide copies by phone, in person or through the website.

sections.h2: Can I e-record a deed in Hancock County?
sections.html:
Yes. The Hancock County Recorder accepts electronic documents of every type, including deeds that need the Auditor's conveyance step. Four outside services are used to submit them, and the office's page lists them by name.

E-recording is mostly practical for title companies, lenders and attorneys. An individual selling a house can ask the closing attorney or title office whether the deed will go electronically, since those firms already hold accounts with the services.

faqs.q: Will the Hancock County Recorder add or remove a name on my deed?
faqs.a: Not without a new deed. The Recorder says adding or removing someone, or changing a name, takes a newly prepared deed, and the office only records documents. It suggests an attorney or title office to prepare it.

faqs.q: Who holds my original deed after I pay off my mortgage in Hancock County?
faqs.a: Neither the Recorder nor your bank holds the original deed during the loan. You should get it back shortly after closing, so contact the attorney or title office that handled the sale. If it is lost, the Recorder can make a copy.

faqs.q: Does the Hancock County Recorder provide blank deed forms?
faqs.a: No. The office does not give out blank deeds, mortgages, liens or other real property forms, and it recommends an attorney or title office for preparation.

faqs.q: How much is the Hancock County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Recorder's FAQ lists $3.00 per thousand for the Auditor's conveyance fee and $0.50 per parcel for the transfer fee. Confirm the total with the Auditor before you pay.

faqs.q: What time must I get a deed to the Hancock County Recorder?
faqs.a: By 4:00 pm. The office stays open until 4:30 pm, but recording for the day ends at 4:00 pm and later filings are recorded on the next business day.
